Science.title: Wherever there are people, there is also wildlife—though not necessarily at the same time
Science.summary: Human-induced global change has reached an unprecedented scale and intensity. Through intensive land use and the associated loss of species, humans are permanently altering the habitats and communities of wild animals. "How do predators manage to find their way in landscapes heavily shaped by humans and establish their niche? It is precisely this question that interested us," says Kathi Kasper, a doctoral student at the MRI PAS, the EBD-CSIC and the Leibniz-IZW and an author of the study.

Science.title: Using vibrations to reveal what lies beneath other planets' surfaces
Science.summary: Modern space exploration hasn't quite reached "Star Trek" levels of boldly going where no one has gone before. But if, like the denizens of the USS Enterprise, astronauts one day want to land on an uncharted planet, they'd first want to know what's on—and under—the surface.

Science.title: Tiny fossils show brittle stars gathered around a dead whale 9.5 million years ago
Science.summary: Tiny skeletal plates recovered beside fossil whale bones in southern Denmark offer a rare glimpse of life around a whale carcass approximately 9.5 million years ago. Researchers have identified a new species of brittle star, Ophiura huebnerjenseni, from the Gram Clay Pit and suggest it represents the first fossil record of brittle stars associated with a whale fall.

Science.title: Astronaut and Earth
Science.summary: CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk is pictured during the Oct. 29, 2026, spacewalk. The International Space Station was soaring 267 miles above the South Atlantic Ocean at the time of this photograph. Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon installed a new roll-out solar array on the space station and performed some get-ahead work […]

Science.title: Biotech firms are meant to pay to use Earth’s genetic data. They’re not.
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03554-6 Global leaders at COP17 biodiversity summit complained that companies using public genetic data are not paying into a voluntary fund to protect nature.

Science.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

Science.title: The marginalia found in millions of Arabic manuscripts could reshape our understanding of Islamic history
Science.summary: For a comprehensive understanding of the content of millions of Arabic manuscripts held in libraries around the world, it is crucial for scholars to first examine what their marginalia reveal, according to a new study published in the Journal of Islamic Thought and Civilization.

Science.title: Researchers develop method for single-cell DNA methylation analysis
Science.summary: Researchers have recently developed a standardized workflow for analyzing DNA methylation in individual cells. The protocol combines an improved laboratory procedure with an automated data analysis tool, making it easier to study differences between cells. Published in Nature Protocols, the study was led by researchers from the Institute of Health and Medical Technology at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Science.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
Science.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.

Science.title: Ancient star collisions could explain mysterious Little Red Dots and 'impossible' black holes
Science.summary: Collisions between stars in the early universe were common, and this could explain the growth of supermassive black holes and the existence of strange Little Red Dots seen by the James Webb Space Telescope.

Science.title: NASA asks industry for ideas about saving Hubble Space Telescope
Science.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope is healthy but is being pulled down toward Earth by atmospheric drag. NASA is considering options to extend the iconic telescope's work.

Science.title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
Science.summary: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue. But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago. Science.title: Disillusion runs deep among young Americans, poll reveals
Science.summary: The kids are not all right on the future. For the first time in the 26-year history of the Harvard Youth Poll, more respondents expect to be worse off financially than their parents (27%) than better off (25%).

Science.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
Science.summary: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

Science.title: Hubble Telescope sees cosmic 'cat's tail' that could wrap around Earth and the sun 500 times
Science.summary: Using the Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have investigated a cosmic cat's tail formed when two Pluto-sized bodies smashed together.

Science.title: Research bonuses need clear and fair rules
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03562-6 Research bonuses need clear and fair rules

Science.title: Scarcer food may have pushed early humans to rework stone tools for longer use
Science.summary: About 300,000 years ago, the emergence of the first Homo sapiens in Africa was accompanied by major cultural and technological changes, marking the beginning of a new archaeological period, the Middle Stone Age. At that time, African landscapes were also undergoing profound transformations. To understand how the earliest members of our species lived and adapted, it is therefore essential to reconstruct the environments in which they lived.

Science.title: Southern Ocean waters reveal distinct nutrient recycling pathways during decades-long journeys north
Science.summary: The Southern Ocean may seem far removed from the North Pacific or the Gulf of Maine, but its waters are linked to all the world's major ocean basins through a vast circulation system.

Science.title: Tijuana River pollution doesn't stay put—it can travel seven times farther than expected
Science.summary: Waste dumped into the Tijuana River can travel seven times farther than expected before becoming airborne and affecting San Diego's air, at least 20 miles (32 kilometers) from its source, according to new UC Riverside research.

Science.title: Talk of the town: Virtual world gets stroke survivors talking
Science.summary: Have you ever felt like you know exactly what you want to say, but just can't get the words out? Having a word on the tip of your tongue can be frustrating at the best of times, but for people with communication difficulties, it can be a constant struggle to find the right words, make sentences and connect with others.

Science.title: More power, less payoff: Study reveals a bottleneck in cleaner methanol production
Science.summary: Dialing up the power on electricity-driven chemical reactions doesn't guarantee that they'll be more efficient, suggests a new study, a finding that gets researchers closer to creating the ideal conditions for sustainable chemical manufacturing.

Science.title: The Star Wars Eclipse — Want to see the 2027 total solar eclipse on Tatooine? Head to Tunisia
Science.summary: From Mos Eisley to Mos Espa and the Jundland Wastes, here's where to experience the Aug. 2, 2027 total solar eclipse from Tunisia's Star Wars filming locations.

Science.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
Science.summary: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

Science.title: Why does Betelgeuse keep fading? The mystery of Orion's giant star
Science.summary: From stellar pulsations to giant dust clouds and a mysterious companion, astronomers are piecing together why Betelguese keeps changing brightness.

Science.title: Plant-inspired natural coatings can beat forever chemicals
Science.summary: Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are known as "forever chemicals" because of the impact they make on the environment and human bodies. Much of modern manufacturing relies on these substances for safe packaging, fire protection and waterproof coatings.

Science.title: As it gets harder to figure out what to eat, some Americans are turning to religion for answers
Science.summary: It's getting harder and harder to figure out what to eat. A scroll through social media raises many questions. Why is food so expensive? Am I getting enough protein? What about fiber? Do I need supplements? Should I be making all my bread at home? What foods were recalled this week?

Science.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
Science.summary: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.

Science.title: Body size, not competition, may kick-start evolution
Science.summary: A new evolutionary theory suggests changes in body size, rather than competition for food and habitat, may drive the earliest physical differences between species.

Science.title: How humans influence fish behavior and why this is important for species conservation
Science.summary: Two recent review articles in the journals Trends in Ecology & Evolution and Fish and Fisheries, to which researchers from the Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB) contributed, focus on the influence of humans on the diversity of fish behavior and on how management can help preserve this diversity.

Science.title: Finding the fingerprints of noisy distributions in random quantum systems
Science.summary: Imagine shuffling a deck of cards where some of the cards are fading just because of the way they interact with the external environment as you shuffle them. Your job is to figure out the interplay between the shuffling, or "imposed randomness," due to the way you shuffle your cards and how that relates to the fading as cards are exposed to the external environment.

Science.title: Single-copy genes can be used as markers to distinguish between bacteria in the same family
Science.summary: The more than 100 bacterial species of the genus Vibrio are important in marine ecosystems because they contribute to the carbon cycle and other ecological processes, but they can also be significant pathogens for both humans (they can cause cholera) and animals (they can drastically reduce productivity in fish and crustacean farms [e.g., prawns] or cause coral bleaching). Identifying and quantifying Vibrio species in marine and estuarine water samples is complex because identification errors may occur when using molecular methods that lack sufficient resolution.

Science.title: NASA’s CHAPEA Crew “Returns” to Earth
Science.summary: The four-member Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) crew poses outside for the first time in more than a year following the end of their simulated Mars journey on Oct. 31, 2026. Crew members Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right) spent more than a year […]

Science.title: Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
Science.summary: Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart into their fundamental building blocks.

Science.title: Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades
Science.summary: Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades, according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo.

Science.title: When should we listen for alien signals? Scientists turn to game theory
Science.summary: Finding a signal from an extraterrestrial civilization takes more than just pointing a telescope in the right direction. We may also need to listen at exactly the right time.

Science.title: New framework helps turn biodiversity goals into measurable action
Science.summary: The new study by Newcastle University and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) offers a practical roadmap for tracking progress toward halting species extinctions by 2050. It guides users from understanding where species are most at risk in a given area, through taking action to reduce species threats, to measuring the real-world impact of conservation efforts on reducing species extinction risk over time.

Science.title: A 3,200-pound NASA spacecraft could fall to Earth tonight
Science.summary: NASA's Swift Observatory is about to make a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere after a private mission to save it failed. Most of the spacecraft will burn up in orbit.

Science.title: Why we’re setting up an institute for radically broad thinking
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03397-1 The scale of today’s challenges demands a fresh approach — across all disciplines. Here’s how we’re making space for researchers to generate new ideas.

Science.title: Nature awards recognize inspiring women in science
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03545-7 This year’s winners are a materials scientist and a champion of women’s science education. They — like all those shortlisted — are driven by the desire to support others.

Science.title: Cold storage can extend shelf life of platelets for dogs facing life-threatening bleeding
Science.summary: Veterinarians often have limited access to one of the most effective tools for controlling life-threatening bleeding complications in dogs: platelets.

Science.title: A single measurement makes quantum bits more reliable
Science.summary: Researchers at the University of Regensburg and their international partners have found a way to significantly reduce errors in quantum bits. In an experiment, they demonstrated that a single additional measurement before a series of quantum operations can cut the error rate by more than half. The results have been published in Applied Physics Reviews.

Science.title: New 'Star Trek: The Original Voyages' book traces the stellar legacy of the bold sci-fi brand
Science.summary: Keep the 60th anniversary party going with this visual salute to the series that launched a legacy

Science.title: A laser can draw superconductivity at the nanoscale
Science.summary: Researchers from ICMAB-CSIC, the Politecnico di Milano and Université de Liège have adapted a direct laser writing technique that allows them to "draw" superconducting properties in a material. The result is a new way to locally program the behavior of a superconductor, tuning it from a fully superconducting state to an insulating one with extraordinary precision.

Science.title: Traces of ancient blood found in 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil, new study claims
Science.summary: Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

Science.title: Asymmetric atomic structure improves sodium–sulfur battery performance
Science.summary: Chinese researchers have developed a new way to improve sodium–sulfur battery performance by changing the atomic structure of a catalyst. Led by professors Wang Hui and Zheng Fangcai from the High Magnetic Field Laboratory at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the study is published in Angewandte Chemie.

Science.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
Science.summary: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Science.title: Mars-bound astronauts could face years of heart scarring, rat study hints
Science.summary: Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

Science.title: Whence dragons?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03277-8 The ecology and evolution of winged legendary beasts, and monkeys that show their behinds to their buddies, in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

Science.title: Would you risk your health to visit Mars?
Science.summary: A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.

Science.title: Improved asteroid deflection model runs faster, reveals more doomsday worries
Science.summary: “We expected aim to matter ... What surprised us was how much,' says Sandia physicist Nathan Moore
